 A Democratic win in the Nevada governor race could unlock dozens of twice-vetoed bills
 Nevada State Legislature in Carson City, Nevada Wednesday, April 27, 2022. Photo by:
 Wade Vandervort 
 By
 Ray Brewer
 ( contact )
 Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 | 2 a.m.
 Editor's note: Este artículo está traducido al español. 
 Twice, Nevada lawmakers passed a bill capping prescription drug prices at Medicare levels. Twice, Gov. Joe Lombardo vetoed it.
 The same fate met a cap on rent increases for seniors, a ban on people under 21 owning semiautomatic rifles and at least eight other bills the Republican governor rejected in 2023 and again in 2025. They were among a state-record 87 vetoes that year.
 Tuesday’s election could break that cycle.
 If Democrats keep their legislative majorities, as forecasters expect, and Attorney General Aaron Ford defeats Lombardo, Democrats would control the governor’s office and both legislative chambers for the first time since January 2023. Polls show a dead heat in the governor’s race, with the RealClearPolling average at 42% for each candidate.
 Reviving bills that Lombardo vetoed would be a natural starting point for a Democratic agenda when the Legislature convenes Feb. 1 in Carson City. Ford has said he would sign several within his first 30 days, including the drug-price cap, universal free school meals and limits on corporate homebuying.
 Lombardo counters that his vetoes protected Nevadans from costly mandates, warning that a Democratic sweep would mean higher taxes.
 Here are scenarios for the 2027 Legislature, regardless of who wins the governor’s race:
 The likeliest early bills 
 Several bills that returned in 2025 were rewritten to answer Lombardo’s earlier objections. The changes did not alter the outcome.
 • Prescription drug prices: Assembly Bill 259 (2025) would have capped prices at the maximums Medicare sets under the federal Inflation Reduction Act. Lombardo called the 2023 version arbitrary. He said the 2025 bill would raise state costs, arguing Medicaid could lose millions in drug rebates and that it created legal uncertainty for providers.
 • School meals: Lombardo vetoed Assembly Bill 319 (2023), which would have appropriated $43 million to continue universal free breakfast and lunch in Nevada public schools . His office said about 87% of schools already serve free meals to all students. The 2025 follow-up, Assembly Bill 268, initially sought $86 million over two years.
 • Corporate homebuying: Senate Bill 395 (2023), sponsored by Sen. Dina Neal, D-North Las Vegas, would have capped corporate investors at 1,000 homes a year. Lombardo vetoed it as arbitrary. Neal’s 2025 version, Senate Bill 391, cut the cap to 100 but needed a two-thirds Senate vote and fell one short after Sen. Ira Hansen, R-Sparks, voted no. Hansen said Lombardo’s office had asked Republican senators to oppose it. A similar measure also failed in the November 2025 special session.
 • Senior rent cap: Ford says he would not sign legislation establishing general rent control but would sign a seniors’ cap. Lombardo vetoed a 10% version in 2023. Assembly Bill 280 (2025) shrank it to a 5% limit on annual increases in a roughly one-year pilot, but Lombardo said caps could discourage rental investment and prompt landlords to raise rents early.
 Other vetoed legislation that could return 
 • Healthcare: Senate Bill 217 (2025) would have codified a right to in vitro fertilization and required most insurers, including Medicaid, to cover it. Lombardo said he backs IVF access but the state can’t afford the Medicaid mandate. Also vetoed: nurse-to-patient ratios at hospitals in Clark and Washoe counties (Senate Bill 182); a ban on insurers relying solely on artificial intelligence to deny prior authorizations (Senate Bill 128); and medical-debt collection limits (Assembly Bill 204), which Lombardo rejected again as an intrusion into private contracts.
 • Labor: Assembly Bill 388 would have required employers with 50 or more workers to offer 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave a year. Also vetoed: higher wage-garnishment protections (Senate Bill 142); waiting-time penalties for unpaid wages (Senate Bill 198); and teacher bargaining over class sizes (Assembly Bill 155).
 • Tenants: Bills that would have overhauled Nevada’s summary eviction process (Assembly Bill 283), allowed tenants to withhold rent if landlords fail to make needed repairs (Assembly Bill 223) and automatically sealed eviction cases (Assembly Bill 201).
 • Elections: Assembly Bill 306, from Assembly Speaker Steve Yeager, would have required county clerks in certain counties to keep mail ballot drop boxes available between the end of early voting and Election Day. Lombardo vetoed it in May 2025 for lacking oversight. Assembly Bill 597 would have let nonpartisan voters, the state’s largest bloc, opt in to vote in a major party’s primary, except presidential primaries.
 Senate Bill 102 would have made it a crime to submit a false slate of presidential electors. Democrats passed it in response to six Nevada Republicans who signed a fake certificate in 2020 awarding the state’s electoral votes to Donald Trump, part of a coordinated effort in several swing states to overturn Joe Biden’s victory. Sen. Skip Daly, D-Sparks, lowered the prison term to 1-4 years from 4-10 years and dropped a ban on public employment. Lombardo vetoed it again, this time calling it overbroad and a First Amendment risk.
 • Guns: For the second consecutive session, Lombardo vetoed a ban on people under 21 owning semiautomatic rifles and shotguns (Assembly Bill 245), calling it “strikingly similar” to the 2023 bill and saying it likely wouldn’t survive U.S. Supreme Court precedent. Bills banning guns within 100 feet of election sites (Assembly Bill 105) and barring people convicted of hate crimes from possessing guns (Senate Bill 89) were also vetoed twice.
 • Immigration and social issues: Limits on federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at schools (Assembly Bill 217), a ban on book bans (Assembly Bill 416) , opt-out sex education (Assembly Bill 205) and a shield law for gender-affirming care providers (Senate Bill 171) were vetoed in both sessions. Sen. James Ohrenschall, D-Las Vegas, rewrote his shield law to mirror the reproductive-care shield Lombardo signed in 2023. It was vetoed anyway.
 Making the legislative sausage 
 A vetoed bill does not automatically become law under a new governor. Each would have to be reintroduced, heard and passed again during the 120-day session that begins Feb. 1.
 Nevada’s Constitution requires two-thirds of each chamber to approve legislation that raises revenue. Democrats hold 13 of 21 Senate seats and 27 of 42 Assembly seats, one short of two-thirds in each.
 Even a two-thirds majority doesn’t guarantee Democrats would agree on every bill. Assemblymember Tracy Brown-May, D-Las Vegas, and Sen. Roberta Lange, D-Las Vegas, voted against paid family leave. Five Senate Democrats opposed the voter ID compromise. Neal joined Republicans against open primaries.
 Money could be another constraint. Lombardo cited cost in several vetoes, including IVF, school meals and state-employee benefits. Federal Medicaid changes and a weaker revenue picture could squeeze a Ford budget, too.
 Opposition from outside the Legislature would also remain. Hospitals fought nurse ratios, business groups fought paid leave and landlords fought tenant bills. The under-21 gun ban and the drug-price cap also carry litigation risk.
 Deliberate checks 
 Lombardo presents his vetoes as a deliberate check. In a June 13, 2025, statement, he said he doesn’t enjoy using the veto, but that his job is to stop legislation that goes too far, grows the government or hurts families and businesses.
 He has pledged no new taxes and calls himself a check on the Democratic Legislature. His campaign also points to $2 billion in new funding during his term, $183 million for housing and a bipartisan housing law now funding new homes.
 Two exceptions show that similar measures he vetoed in 2023 became law in 2025.
 Lombardo signed Assembly Bill 530 in 2025, which lets the Clark County Commission continue indexing fuel taxes to inflation with a two-thirds vote. He vetoed a nearly identical bill in 2023.
 He also signed Assembly Bill 96, an urban heat mitigation measure similar to one he vetoed in 2023. It requires counties and cities with populations over 100,000 to include a heat mitigation plan in the conservation element of their master plans.
